title: Settings in a billing tool
excerpt: Billing settings are a cabinet, not a second product. Group the footer, tax, and reminders a finance lead changes, and bury the rest.
alt: A hand holding a blue pen over wireframe sketches, with a mug and a closed notebook nearby, a plan being marked before it is put away.
caption: A hand marking wireframe sketches, decisions made and then set aside. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in the front of billing settings?
faqs.answer: The things a finance lead changes when they are afraid of a wrong invoice: the footer note, the tax treatment, the reminder schedule, and the default currency. Those affect the next send. Processor keys, webhook URLs, and chart-of-accounts mapping belong in a deeper drawer, usually for an admin, not on the way to the footer.

faqs.question: Should settings be a separate product area with its own home?
faqs.answer: Open a cabinet, change the one control, and return to the invoice that was open. A settings home with charts, tours, and a marketplace pulls the lead away from the draft they were checking. The invoice is the product, and settings are only the drawer.

faqs.question: How do we stop a setting from changing invoices already sent?
faqs.answer: Say whether the change affects future invoices only. A footer edit that rewrites sent PDFs is a surprise no lead wants. Preview the next invoice. Leave the sent ones stable unless they explicitly choose to regenerate, and even then name the count.

markdown:
Billing tool settings UX is a cabinet, not a second product. Group what the finance lead, the one who is afraid of a wrong invoice, changes often: the footer, the tax, the reminders, the currency. Bury processor keys, webhook URLs, and anything that is really an engineering connection. Then send them back to the invoice they were checking.

If settings has a dashboard, the cabinet has already become a lobby, and lobbies are where the wrong default survives.

## The drawer that changes the next send

The lead opens settings because something on the invoice looks wrong, or because they want to stop it from looking wrong next time. The first drawer should be those controls, and almost nothing else.

Footer and memo. The note that appears on the PDF: payment terms, a purchase-order line, a legal sentence. They change it the week a lawyer asks, or the week a customer disputes the terms. Show a preview of the next invoice, not a raw text area with no sense of the page. "This appears under the total on invoices you send after saving. It does not change invoices already sent." That second sentence is the whole trust of the control. If you cannot say it, do not ship the control until you can.

Tax. The default rate, whether prices include it, and which customers are exceptions. A single "tax mode" dropdown with internal names is how a wrong invoice gets scheduled. Label the choices as outcomes. "Add tax on top of the line items" and "Prices already include tax." Show an example with a round number. If a change would alter drafts that are scheduled, list them before they save. "3 scheduled invoices would be recalculated." Let them open the list. A save that silently rewrites scheduled totals is the fear, automated.

Reminders. When a reminder goes out, and the sentence it uses. This is a customer-facing setting hiding in a cabinet. Preview the email with a real invoice's amount and a fake send. Default to a modest cadence. A lead who is afraid of being wrong is also afraid of nagging the wrong customer. Show which statuses can be reminded. Never remind a void. Never remind a draft. Say that next to the toggle so they do not have to discover it from a customer's reply.

Currency. The default for new invoices, stated as a code, with an example. Changing the default must not convert existing drafts without a preview. Conversion is a different, dangerous action. Keep it out of this toggle. "New invoices will use USD. Existing drafts stay as they are." If that is not true of your implementation, change the implementation before you write a softer label.

## A cabinet they can leave

Open settings from the invoice, and return to that invoice on save and on cancel. The unsaved lines they were reviewing have to be there. A settings flow that drops them on a home screen teaches them never to fix a footer in the middle of a check, which means the footer stays wrong. The path is the feature.

Do not celebrate the save. "Footer updated. It will be on the next send." is enough. A full-page success illustration is the second product again.

[The WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) applies to web applications and organizes quality as perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Settings pages fail understandable more often than almost any other screen, because the labels were written by the people who built the storage. "remit_memo_v2" is not a label. "Note under the total" is. Group the four frequent controls. Give each a description of what changes and what does not. Make sure a keyboard can reach them in the same order the eye uses. A finance lead on a bad morning is not a reason to require a precise cursor.

Name the drawers in outcomes, not in your architecture. "What customers see." "Tax and currency." "Reminders." The deeper door can be "Connections," and it can be labeled as affecting payouts and engineers, so a lead does not wander in while looking for the footer.

## What a wrong default costs

Defaults are the invoices you will send when nobody opens the cabinet. Set them as if the lead is on leave. A default reminder that fires on drafts will fire. A default currency taken from a browser locale will bill a domestic customer in the wrong unit the week someone demos the tool from a laptop overseas. Pick the company's currency explicitly during setup, then leave locale out of it.

Review defaults with one question: if we never open this again, is the next invoice acceptable? If the answer is no, the default is unfinished, and a setting is being used as a substitute for a decision. Make the decision. Then expose the control for the exception.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks for trust on topics that can affect financial stability, and it asks you not to leave people needing another search to finish the job. A setting that requires a help article to avoid a wrong tax treatment is an unfinished label. Put the example on the control. The help article can exist. It should not be required to send a correct invoice.

Write the default next to the control in the interface, not only in your docs. "Default: tax added on top." When someone changes it, the new value becomes visible on the next invoice preview before they leave the cabinet. If the preview and the control disagree, the preview wins and the control is a bug. Do not ship a cabinet where those two can drift.

## Bury the connections

Processor keys, webhook endpoints, API tokens, and the mapping to an accounting export are not the lead's frequent job. They are sharp. They belong in a drawer that says changes here can stop payouts or duplicate events. An admin or an engineer can open it. The lead should not scroll through it to reach reminders.

If the lead must reconnect a payout account, make that a task with a start and a finish, not a form of raw keys. "Payout account needs attention" can surface on the first screen as a status, and the task can live in this buried drawer. Do not paste the whole drawer onto the invoice. The invoice stays about the customer. The connection stays about the company.

Logos of other products, arranged as a marketplace, do not belong in the first drawer and barely belong in the second. Each logo is an invitation to leave the invoice. If an integration is required for tax calculation, it is not a logo. It is a status: "Tax calculation is connected" or "Tax calculation is off, so send is blocked." Status is what the lead needed. The marketplace is what a partnership team needed. They can have a page. It should not be the cabinet's front.

Export to an accountant is a task, not a setting. "Send this month's paid invoices" with a preview of the count. Put it where the month-end work happens. A checkbox called "enable export" that does nothing visible is how the cabinet fills with dead controls.

## The week something changes

There is a week when the footer must change, a tax rule changes, or reminders are paused because of a known incident. The cabinet should make that week boring. One drawer. A preview. A sentence about what will not change, which is the sent archive. A list of scheduled invoices if they would change. A save.

Pause is a first-class control for reminders and for scheduled sends. "Pause all scheduled sends" is extreme and sometimes correct. It should be available without a hunt, it should state how many invoices are held, and it should be obvious how to resume. A pause buried under connections will not be found in the hour it is needed. That hour is why the control exists. Put pause next to reminders and next to the idea of scheduled sends, and require a confirmation that names the count. "Hold 6 scheduled invoices. Nothing already sent will be recalled." Recalling sent mail is a different feature and usually a fantasy. Do not imply it.

After the week, the lead should be able to see what they changed. A short log in the admin drawer, "footer updated Tuesday," is enough. It is not a compliance product unless you are actually building one. It is a way to answer "who changed the terms" without a forensic reading of the PDF archive. If you cannot offer a log, at least show "last changed" on the control. Amnesia in a cabinet is how two people "fix" the same footer in opposite directions.

## What engineering owns

Engineering owns the keys, the retries, the idempotency of webhooks, and the guarantee that a footer change does not rewrite history. The interface owns the promise that those guarantees are visible. When engineering and the label disagree, the lead will believe the label and the ledger will believe engineering. That gap is a wrong invoice even if every screen looks calm.

Hanabi builds product interfaces in the same stack as the marketing sites when the product is a web app: Next.js, React, TypeScript, and a database in PostgreSQL when the data needs to be real. The stack will not decide which drawer is first. The design has to. Do that decision in Figma with the invoice beside the cabinet, and refuse a screen that cannot show the effect on the next send. If a control's effect cannot be previewed, it is not ready for the lead.

Do not let a design system treat settings as an unstyled form dumped from a schema. The components for a dangerous select, a preview, and a "future only" notice are as important as the button on the invoice. Build them once. Use them on tax, currency, and reminders. A one-off dropdown is how "includes tax" gets a different meaning on two screens.

## How you know it became a second product

Count the clicks from a scheduled invoice to the footer preview and back. If it is more than a few, or if the path visits a marketplace, the cabinet is too proud. Watch a lead pause reminders. If they ask where send settings went, you have split one idea across two drawers and named them for your org chart.

Listen for spreadsheet workarounds. A footer maintained in a doc and pasted into each invoice means the cabinet lost. Bring the sentence back into the first drawer and make the preview trustworthy. People abandon settings when the preview lied once. They will not tell you in a survey. They will just paste.

Keep the first drawer to what customers see, tax, currency, and reminders. Anything else has to be part of the next send. A cabinet that grows with every roadmap item will hide the footer, and the footer is why this screen exists.

The same need for one object and one action shows up when someone is trying to book a time rather than check a number. [The first screen of a scheduling product](/blog/the-first-screen-of-a-scheduling-product) is the next piece, because the person who just wants a time, not an account, should see that time and one action, not a tour of the product.

[Selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is a look at interfaces Hanabi has designed and built with that kind of restraint.
